module.title: Functions
module.description: Functions: domain, codomain, range; injective, surjective, bijective; inverses; composition; floor and ceiling. v4 adds function_mapping_solution worked examples with explicit injectivity / surjectivity verification and multi-line answers.

lessons.title: Functions — Domain, Codomain, Range
lessons.welcome: A FUNCTION is the most fundamental machine in mathematics: feed it an input, get exactly one output. Functions structure programming, model real-world maps, and underpin every later topic.
objectives: Define a function as an assignment from a domain to a codomain.
Identify domain, codomain, and range; distinguish the last two.
Decide whether a given relation is a function.
Recognize special functions (identity, constant, floor, ceiling).
Use function notation correctly: f: A → B, f(a), f(A').

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: What's the difference between codomain and range?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: The codomain is what you DECLARE — the set of possible outputs. The range is what you ACTUALLY HIT — the subset of the codomain that the function reaches. They're equal only when the function is surjective. Always range ⊆ codomain.

flow.title: Function
flow.content: A **function** f from a set A to a set B, written f: A → B, assigns to **each** element of A exactly **one** element of B. A is the **domain**; B is the **codomain**. The element assigned to a is f(a) (the **image** of a under f).

flow.title: Range (image)
flow.content: The **range** of f is the set of all output values f actually produces: range(f) = {f(a) | a ∈ A}. Always range(f) ⊆ codomain(f), but the two are not always equal.

flow.title: Function vs not-a-function (the rules)
rows: Every element of A has an image
Some a ∈ A has no f(a)
Every element of A has only ONE image
Some a maps to two different outputs
flow.notes: If either rule fails, the assignment is a relation, not a function.

flow.title: Functions around campus and on Absher
items: **Student → Student ID** at KAU: every student is assigned exactly one ID. Function ✓.
**Course → Instructor** for a given semester: each course has one instructor. Function ✓ (range may be smaller than the set of all KAU faculty).
**Iqama → Vehicles registered**: an iqama can have several cars on Absher → NOT a function (multiple outputs per input). It's a relation.
**Phone number → Owner** on STC: each number maps to one subscriber. Function ✓.

flow.title: Image of a subset
flow.content: For S ⊆ A, the **image** of S under f is f(S) = {f(s) | s ∈ S}. The range is just f(A) — the image of the entire domain.

flow.title: Floor on negative numbers
flow.content: **⌊-2.3⌋ = -3, NOT -2.** Floor goes DOWN; for negatives, that means more negative. Check on a number line if unsure.

flow.title: Is it a function?
flow.problem: A = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Decide if each is a function from A to ℤ: (a) f(x) = x². (b) g(x) = ±√x. (c) h with h(1) = 5 only. (d) k(x) = ⌊x/2⌋.
flow.thinking_process: Check totality (every input has an output) and single-valued (one output per input).
step_by_step_solution: (a) Each x has unique x². Function ✓.
(b) g(4) could be 2 or -2 — two outputs. NOT a function.
(c) h(2), h(3), h(4) undefined. NOT a function (not total).
(d) k(1)=0, k(2)=1, k(3)=1, k(4)=2. Each input one output. Function ✓.
flow.common_mistake: Calling g a function — multi-valued assignments are relations, not functions.

flow.title: Domain, codomain, range
flow.problem: Let f: ℤ → ℤ, f(x) = x². Identify domain, codomain, range.
flow.thinking_process: Domain and codomain are declared; range is computed.
step_by_step_solution: Domain: ℤ.
Codomain: ℤ (declared).
Range: {0, 1, 4, 9, 16, …} = squares of integers ⊆ ℤ. Range ≠ codomain.
flow.final_answer: Domain ℤ, codomain ℤ, range = {n² : n ∈ ℤ}.
flow.common_mistake: Confusing range with codomain — only equal when f is surjective.

flow.title: Floor and ceiling
flow.thinking_process: Floor goes down; ceiling goes up. Integers are unchanged.
step_by_step_solution: ⌊3.7⌋ = 3 (greatest integer ≤ 3.7).
⌈3.7⌉ = 4 (smallest integer ≥ 3.7).
⌊-3.7⌋ = -4 (more negative).
⌈-3.7⌉ = -3 (less negative).
flow.common_mistake: Thinking ⌊-3.7⌋ = -3. Floor goes DOWN, which on negatives means more negative.

flow.title: Common student mistakes
items: Equating range with codomain.
Calling a multi-valued assignment a function.
Forgetting that functions must be TOTAL (every domain element has an image).
Floor of a negative going the wrong way.

flow.title: Quick checks
items: **Total + single-valued = function.**
**Range ⊆ codomain.**
**Floor goes DOWN, ceiling goes UP.**
**(Negatives flip the direction of 'down'.)**

sections.heading: What is a function
sections.explanation: Total + single-valued assignment from domain to codomain.

step_by_step_solution: g(4) = ±2 — two outputs. NOT a function.

quick_checks.question: f: ℤ → ℤ, f(x) = x². Range:

quick_checks.explanation: Floor goes more negative for negatives.

quick_checks.question: Range always equals codomain.
quick_checks.explanation: Equal only when f is surjective.

key_takeaways: Function = total + single-valued assignment from domain to codomain.
Range ⊆ codomain; equality only when surjective.
Identity, constant, floor, ceiling are key special functions.
On negatives: floor goes more negative; ceiling less negative.

lessons.title: Injective, Surjective, Bijective — and Composition
lessons.welcome: Functions can be classified by how they relate inputs to outputs. Three labels (injective, surjective, bijective) describe everything you need to know about invertibility and composition.
objectives: Decide which label applies to a given function.
Define and compute the inverse of a bijection.
Compute the composition of two functions.
Recognize that a function is invertible iff it is bijective.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: How do I check injectivity from a formula?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Show that f(a) = f(b) forces a = b. Algebraically: assume f(a) = f(b), then derive a = b. If you cannot, look for two different inputs producing the same output — that's a counterexample.

flow.title: Injective (one-to-one)
flow.content: f is **injective** iff different inputs always give different outputs: `∀a, b ∈ A (a ≠ b → f(a) ≠ f(b))`. Equivalently: `f(a) = f(b) → a = b`.

flow.title: Surjective (onto)
flow.content: f: A → B is **surjective** iff every element of B has a pre-image: `∀b ∈ B ∃a ∈ A (f(a) = b)`. Equivalently: range(f) = B.

flow.title: Bijective (one-to-one correspondence)
flow.content: f is **bijective** iff it is BOTH injective AND surjective. Bijections pair up A and B element-by-element.

flow.title: Quick decision
rows: Are any two domain elements sent to the same output? If no → injective
Is range = codomain? If yes → surjective

flow.title: Three example functions on small sets
Saudi-flavoured examples
items: **Student → Student ID** at KAU: injective (no two students share an ID) but not surjective onto all 9-digit numbers (only the IDs actually issued).
**Saudi car plate → Owner**: injective (one plate, one owner). Not surjective onto everyone in Saudi Arabia (most people don't own a car).
**Day of the year → Day-of-week (Sun..Sat)**: surjective (every weekday is hit) but not injective (multiple days share the same weekday).
**Iqama → Resident** (one-to-one valid mapping): bijective when domain is set of all current residents and codomain is set of issued iqamas.

flow.title: Inverse function
flow.content: If f: A → B is **bijective**, the inverse f⁻¹: B → A is defined by f⁻¹(b) = the unique a with f(a) = b. Only bijections have inverses. f⁻¹ is also bijective and (f⁻¹)⁻¹ = f.

flow.trigger: After inverses — students often think every function has an inverse.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: Why doesn't f(x) = x² over ℝ have an inverse?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: It is not bijective on ℝ. It fails injectivity (since f(2) = f(-2) = 4) AND surjectivity onto ℝ (since negatives have no real square root). Restrict to ℝ⁺ → ℝ⁺ and now x² IS bijective; its inverse is √x.

flow.title: Composition
flow.content: Given f: A → B and g: B → C, the **composition** g ∘ f: A → C is defined by `(g ∘ f)(a) = g(f(a))`. Read right-to-left: f first, then g. Composition is **associative** but NOT commutative in general.

flow.title: Properties under composition
headers: If f and g are both …

flow.title: Decide the label — f(n) = 2n + 3 over ℤ
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 09 Q3 — classify a given function.
flow.problem: Let f: ℤ → ℤ, f(n) = 2n + 3. Determine whether f is injective, surjective, and/or bijective.
flow.approach: Test injectivity by f(a) = f(b) ⇒ a = b. Test surjectivity onto ℤ by solving f(n) = m for arbitrary m ∈ ℤ.

checks.argument: Assume f(a) = f(b). Then 2a + 3 = 2b + 3 ⇒ 2a = 2b ⇒ a = b. ✓
We need n ∈ ℤ with 2n + 3 = m, i.e., n = (m − 3)/2. For odd m (e.g., m = 4: n = 1/2 ∉ ℤ), no integer solution. ✗

step_by_step_solution: **Step 1 (Injective check)** — Assume f(a) = f(b): 2a + 3 = 2b + 3 ⇒ a = b. ✓
**Step 2 (Surjective check onto ℤ)** — Solve f(n) = m for n: n = (m − 3)/2. For m = 4 this is 1/2 ∉ ℤ — fails. ✗
**Step 3 (Bijective check)** — bijective = injective ∧ surjective. Surjectivity fails, so bijection fails.
flow.final_answer:
**Injective:** Yes.
**Surjective onto ℤ:** No (odd targets have no integer preimage).
**Bijective:** No.
flow.why_it_works: Each property has a precise definition; we test each separately and combine.
flow.common_mistake: Forgetting that surjectivity depends on the codomain — over ℝ, f WOULD be surjective.

flow.title: Find the inverse of f(x) = 3x − 7 over ℝ
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 09 Q4 — inverse of a linear function.
flow.problem: Let f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = 3x − 7. Verify f is bijective and find f⁻¹.
flow.approach: Check both properties first (only bijections have inverses), then solve y = f(x) for x to obtain f⁻¹.

checks.argument: For any y ∈ ℝ, x = (y + 7)/3 ∈ ℝ. ✓

step_by_step_solution: **Step 1 (Injective)** — 3a − 7 = 3b − 7 ⇒ a = b. ✓
**Step 2 (Surjective)** — Solve y = 3x − 7 for x: x = (y + 7)/3 ∈ ℝ for any y ∈ ℝ. ✓
**Step 3 (Inverse)** — Read off f⁻¹: **f⁻¹(y) = (y + 7)/3**.
flow.why_it_works: Bijection ⇔ has an inverse. Solving y = f(x) for x gives the inverse explicitly.
flow.common_mistake: Solving without verifying bijection — an inverse exists only when both injectivity AND surjectivity hold.

flow.title: Composition
flow.problem: Let f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x². Find (g ∘ f)(x) and (f ∘ g)(x).
flow.thinking_process: g ∘ f means f first; substitute f(x) into g.
flow.common_mistake: Reading composition left-to-right. Always: g ∘ f means f first, then g.

flow.title: Common student mistakes
items: Saying every function has an inverse — only bijections do.
Reading composition left-to-right.
Confusing 'one-to-one' (injective) with 'one output per input' (the function definition itself).
Forgetting surjectivity depends on the codomain.

flow.title: Three labels
items: **Injective:** distinct in → distinct out.
**Surjective:** every codomain element is hit.
**Bijective:** both — invertible.
**g ∘ f means f first.**

worked_examples.problem: Is f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = x³ bijective?
step_by_step_solution: Injective: a³ = b³ ⇒ a = b ✓. Surjective: every real has a cube root ✓. Bijective.

quick_checks.explanation: Even outputs only — not surjective onto ℤ.

questions.question: Identity function id(x) is:
A function must be total (every input has an output).

Composition is commutative.

questions.answer: Multi-valued: for x = 4 it gives 2 AND -2.

questions.question: Define injective in your own words.
questions.answer: Distinct inputs produce distinct outputs. Equivalently, f(a) = f(b) forces a = b.

Compute (g ∘ f)(2) and (f ∘ g)(2) for f(x) = x + 1, g(x) = 3x.
Why does floor of a negative go MORE negative?
questions.answer: Floor returns the greatest integer ≤ x. For x = -2.3, the integers ≤ -2.3 are …, -4, -3 — greatest is -3 (more negative than -2.3).

questions.question: f is one-to-one iff f(a) = f(b) ⇒ ___.
f is onto iff range = ___.
f bijective iff f is ___ AND ___.
f is one-to-one iff f(a) = f(b) ⇒ ___.

questions.explanation: On negatives floor goes more negative.

questions.question: Match function to label.
Show f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = (x - 3)/2 is bijective and find f⁻¹.
questions.answer:
Injective: (a-3)/2 = (b-3)/2 ⇒ a = b. ✓
Surjective: for y ∈ ℝ, x = 2y + 3 satisfies f(x) = y. ✓
Bijective. f⁻¹(y) = 2y + 3.

questions.question: Compute (f ∘ g ∘ h)(x) for f(x) = x + 1, g(x) = 2x, h(x) = x².
Decide if f: ℤ → ℤ⁺, f(n) = n² + 1 is injective and/or surjective.
questions.answer:
Injective: f(2) = 5, f(-2) = 5 — same output, different inputs. NOT injective.
Surjective onto ℤ⁺: range = {1, 2, 5, 10, …} = squares + 1; not all positive integers (e.g., 3 not hit). NOT surjective.
Neither.

questions.question: f: ℤ × ℤ → ℤ, f(m, n) = m + n. Is f surjective? Injective?
questions.answer:
Surjective: for any k ∈ ℤ, take (k, 0): f = k. ✓
Injective: f(1, 2) = 3 = f(0, 3). NOT injective.

questions.question: Show that if g ∘ f is injective, then f is injective.
questions.answer: Suppose f(a) = f(b). Apply g: g(f(a)) = g(f(b)), i.e., (g ∘ f)(a) = (g ∘ f)(b). By injectivity of g ∘ f, a = b. So f is injective. ∎

questions.question: Find f⁻¹ for f: ℝ⁺ → ℝ⁺, f(x) = √x.
questions.answer: f(x) = √x bijective on positive reals. y = √x ⇒ x = y². So f⁻¹(y) = y².
questions.explanation: Restrict domain to make it bijective.
